kernels.l1: The overlap holds what is in both hoops. Everything in either hoop, all together, is the big pile.
kernels.l2: Put two hoops on the floor. The overlap is the things in both hoops. Everything in either hoop, counted once, is the whole collection. If the hoops never overlap, nothing is in both.
kernels.l3: S ∪ T, the union, holds everything that is in S or in T or both. S ∩ T, the intersection, holds only what is in both. Union goes with the word or; intersection goes with the word and.
kernels.l4: S ∪ T = {x | x ∈ S ∨ x ∈ T} and S ∩ T = {x | x ∈ S ∧ x ∈ T}. Union is ∨ and intersection is ∧. Always S ⊆ S ∪ T and S ∩ T ⊆ S; disjoint means S ∩ T = ∅.
kernels.l5: Union and intersection are the set-level images of ∨ and ∧; the containments S ∩ T ⊆ S ⊆ S ∪ T hold for all S and T.
kernels.l6: Union collects what lies in at least one of the sets, intersection what lies in both — the set versions of *or* and *and*. The intersection is always inside each set, and each set is always inside the union.
kernels.l7: Union and intersection are defined by disjunction and conjunction of membership conditions; S ∩ T ⊆ S ⊆ S ∪ T always, and S, T are disjoint exactly when S ∩ T = ∅.
kernels.l8: ∪ and ∩ are the join and meet in the Boolean lattice P(X), and they extend to arbitrary indexed families, where the quantifier form ∃i / ∀i replaces ∨ / ∧.
